mainKeyword: robotic pool cleaner for large pools
guideTitle: Best Robotic Pool Cleaners for Large Pools (2026)
metaTitle: Best Robotic Pool Cleaners for Large Pools
metaDescription: Six robotic pool cleaners for large pools compared on battery window, corded reach, filter capacity and coverage claims, with honest limits on each.
expertTake: The Beatbot Sora 70 is the pick for large pools because it pairs a large battery with the broadest coverage claim in the lineup. The Dolphin Nautilus CC Plus Wi-Fi is the reliable value pick for owners who prefer a cable to a battery, and owners of a modest pool should skip every machine here that sells runtime they will not use.
introParagraphs: A large pool changes the arithmetic. The robot has to finish more floor and more wall in a single cycle, so battery window, cable reach and basket capacity stop being footnotes and become the main specifications.

Be sceptical of any coverage claim, because makers quote it under friendly conditions. A sound approach is to measure the water surface, add a margin for the deep end, and prefer designs that can finish a full pass without parking early.

specList.label: Coverage claim

specList.label: Shallow areas

products.description:
The largest battery in this lineup belongs to the Sora 70, and the listing pairs it with a coverage claim of up to 3,200 square feet and up to five hours on floors. On a large pool those two numbers are the point, since a robot that finishes in one go is worth more than one that parks mid-job. It also skims the water surface through jets that push debris toward the machine, which keeps leaves from sinking into the next cycle.

Surface mode costs battery, so the five-hour figure applies to floor cleaning only. It is also the most costly machine here, and a modest pool gains nothing from the extras. Against the Aiper Scuba S1 it offers more raw endurance, while the Aiper counters with finer filtration.

Expect cordless upkeep: charge after every run, rinse the basket, and keep the body shaded because heat ages lithium. Check the surface intakes after leafy runs. Treat the quoted coverage as a ceiling and leave a margin for a long deep end.

products.name: Dolphin Nautilus CC Plus Wi-Fi with scheduling
products.description:
For a large pool, a cable removes the biggest question: will the robot finish? Power arrives through a floating line from a deck transformer, so the machine runs as long as the cycle needs and the schedule can be set once and forgotten. An active brush scrubs the surface as it climbs.

The cost of that certainty is cable management. On a long pool the cable has to reach the far end plus the depth, and a twisted line can drag the robot off its path. Against the Sora 70 it lacks surface skimming and has no cordless freedom, but it never ages a battery.

Uncoil the cable on the deck before each run and let it hang straight. Rinse the top-load basket every cycle, since a large pool fills it faster than a small one does. Keep the transformer sheltered and inspect the brush each season. On a very large pool, ask the seller whether the cable length covers your long axis.
products.bestFor: Large, heavily used pools where finishing every cycle matters most.

products.name: Aiper Scuba S1, eco mode up to 270 minutes

specList.label: Eco runtime
specList.value: Up to 270 minutes through the app

specList.label: Filtration
specList.value: Dual layer with replaceable 3 micron stage

products.description:
Eleven sensors and a dual-path routing algorithm are meant to plan passes so that a big pool is covered evenly instead of in random lines. Route quality matters more as pools grow, because wasted passes burn limited battery. The eco mode stretches runtime to about 270 minutes, which suits a large pool when you are not in a hurry.

Its fine filter layer, rated three microns and replaceable, helps keep large pools clear of silt, though a pool this size generates a lot of debris and the fine mesh will clog fast. Relative to the Sora 70 it has less battery but better filtration, so choose by whether endurance or clarity is your pain point.

Rinse both layers after every run and keep spare layers in the pool box. Charge after each cycle and shade the body. Check the sensors for film now and then.

products.name: Lodoba cordless, dual brushless motors, 190 minutes
products.description:
A pair of brushless motors turning at 3,200 RPM drive a 4,800 GPH suction system, and the lithium pack is listed at up to 190 minutes. Those numbers sit in the middle of the cordless range and cost less than the Sora 70. Three modes let you run floor-only on a big pool to save battery, then do walls on another day.

That modal approach is the practical trick with large pools: split the job so that no single cycle exceeds the battery. The brand is less established, so parts and warranty need a question before purchase. It lists both in-ground and above-ground suitability, so verify wall height for your own pool.

Charge after each run and rinse the basket promptly. Keep the robot shaded and note the model label for filter orders. If your pool is very large, expect to run it twice a week in alternating modes, and write the pattern on the pool box lid so the routine survives a busy summer.
products.bestFor: Large pools on a moderate budget where split-mode cleaning is acceptable.

products.name: TALOSBO C1 with seven app modes

specList.label: Rated area
specList.value: In-ground pools up to 1,615 square feet

products.description:
The TALOSBO C1 is marketed for large in-ground pools, with a stated area of up to 1,615 square feet and a runtime of up to 180 minutes. That area is modest next to the Sora 70 claim, so measure honestly before trusting the label. A triple-motor layout separates drive from suction, and seven app modes let you split a big job into floor, wall and waterline passes.

Its value is a moderate cost for a flexible mode set. Compared with the Lodoba it offers an app and a stated area, while the Lodoba offers a longer stated runtime. Neither should be trusted blindly on coverage claims, and a pool near the TALOSBO limit should run it in alternating modes.

Charge after each run and rinse the filter at once. Keep the pack out of heat. Ask the seller about spare filters and tracks, since a newer brand may not stock them for long and large-pool use wears tracks faster.

products.name: Polaris Freedom Plus cordless, pools to 50 feet
products.description:
Fifty feet is the longest pool this cordless Polaris claims to handle, which makes it the upper limit of its range rather than a promise of ease. It is the choice for large-pool owners who value a dealer network and parts supply over published runtime. The LiFi remote can steer or recall it from the deck.

Versus the Sora 70 it gives up battery and surface cleaning, and compared with the Nautilus CC Plus Wi-Fi it adds cordless freedom with a battery's limits. It costs near the top of the cordless range.

Test the remote battery each spring. Keep the caddy in the shade and charge after every run. Rinse the filter canister promptly. For a pool near fifty feet, plan on splitting the work into shorter cycles.

buyingCriteria.explanation: The Sora 70 lists up to five hours on floors, the Aiper Scuba S1 up to 270 minutes in eco mode, the Lodoba 190 and the TALOSBO C1 180. A large pool needs the whole pass to fit, with a margin of about a third. A robot that parks mid-job leaves the far end dirty. Multiply your usual cycle time before comparing.

The Dolphin Nautilus CC Plus Wi-Fi uses a cable that must reach the far end plus the depth. A cable that barely reaches tugs the robot off line. Measure the long axis and add the deep end. Ask the seller for the cable length before buying.

The Sora 70 quotes up to 3,200 square feet and the Polaris Freedom Plus up to fifty feet, but makers test under friendly conditions. Leaves, algae and slopes cut real coverage. Choose a machine rated comfortably above your pool. A claim at the limit is a claim to doubt.

Large pools collect more debris per cycle, so a small basket fills early and suction drops. Fine layers like the Aiper three micron stage clog fast. A coarse basket rinses easily. Match capacity to the debris load.
The Aiper uses eleven sensors and the Sora 70 uses AI navigation, while gyro robots draw straight lines and drift. Wasted passes burn battery. On big pools, planning is as valuable as capacity.
A large-pool robot works hard and wears parts faster. Polaris and Dolphin have dealer networks, while newer names rely on online sellers. Ask about tracks, brushes and batteries before buying.

Heat ages lithium cells. Charging promptly keeps capacity.
On a long cable, a twist that is never straightened wears the swivel. Straightening it extends life.

faq.q: Which robot suits a large pool best?
faq.a: The Sora 70 offers the largest battery and a surface mode, so it is the best fit for most large pools. Corded buyers should pick the Dolphin Nautilus CC Plus Wi-Fi. Measure your pool first, add the deep end, and pick a machine whose rating clears it with room to spare.

faq.q: Is corded better for large pools?
faq.a: Often, yes, because it never parks early. The cost is cable handling. Cordless works if the battery covers the pass with margin.

faq.q: Can I split cleaning into modes?
faq.a: Yes, models like the Lodoba and TALOSBO C1 let you run floor-only then wall passes. This keeps each cycle inside the battery. It is a good trick on big pools, and it also spreads wear across the brushes and tracks.
Treat them as ceilings. Debris, slopes and algae cut real coverage. Pick a robot rated comfortably above your pool, and treat any claim near your size as a reason to look one step up.

faq.q: How long will the battery last?
faq.a: Expect good performance for several seasons, then gradual fade. Heat speeds it. Long cycles on big pools age packs faster, so a bigger battery that runs at partial depth lasts longer than a small one run flat out.

faq.q: Do I still need my pool filter?
faq.a: Yes. The robot collects debris in its own basket and eases the load on your main filter. It does not circulate or sanitize water.
